passage: Ayesha, sit down, drink your tea. You're angry with your roommate, I can see it. Let me tell you something. When I was twenty, in the nursing hostel in Kochi, I had a best friend called Leelamma. We argued over a borrowed saree she had stained. It got hotter and hotter, and then I said it: "No wonder your father left, look how careless you are." I saw her face go white. My own face burned with shame the same second. I knew I had gone too far. Still, I was proud, and she was angry, and I walked out instead of taking it back. We didn't speak for two years. I'm Kavitha, fifty-four years old, and I still remember her face. Don't let one sentence cost you two years.

Badminton coach's note, college indoor court, Thursday

Jeevan and Mehak, our mixed doubles pair, lost the practice set badly today. At the net they started arguing about the serve.
Then Mehak said, "No wonder your dad's shop shut down. You don't finish anything either." The court went quiet. Jeevan's face went red. He said, "At least my father didn't leave us." Mehak's racquet dropped.
For a second they both looked stunned at themselves, but neither said sorry. Mehak walked off to the bench; Jeevan kept hitting the shuttle against the wall.
I stopped practice, sat each of them down separately, and said we'd talk tomorrow when both were calmer.

qa.a: She said, "No wonder your dad's shop shut down."

The rented room in Sagar had one fan, two cots and a fight that had lasted since dinner.

Abhinav and his cousin Jyoti were preparing for the same state exam. She had cleared the prelims; he hadn't.

"At least I'm not wasting Chacha's money on a second attempt," Jyoti said.

The room went silent. Abhinav's father had taken a loan to send him here; everyone in the family knew.

Abhinav's face burned. "And at least my father didn't lose his shop because he trusted the wrong people," he said.

Jyoti flinched as if he'd slapped her. Her father's shop was the one thing nobody mentioned.

They stared at each other. Abhinav felt sick. He knew it was too far. So did she. But the words "I'm sorry" sat like stones in both their throats, and pride kept them there. Jyoti turned off the light without a word.

qa.a: They were preparing for the same state exam.

qa.a: He felt a flash of anger followed by shame and sickness, knowing it had gone too far, yet pride stopped his apology.
